summary:
Turnout in 2026 is measured against a larger register that also carries more emigrants. The Central Elections Committee lists 7,331,981 eligible voters (+543,177, +8.0% on 2022) and 12,018 polling stations. Election day is a paid day of rest with free intercity transport, as in 2022. About 125,000 net emigrants (January 2022 to August 2024) stay on the roll, which alone lowers measured turnout by about 1.2 points. The national prior (70.5 +/- 2.5) can stay, centred slightly lower; seats follow shares, so little rides on it.

Arab sector. Since the three-party Joint List formed and the Supreme Court reinstated both Arab lists, the estimates tied to the actual configuration cluster at 59-61%. Channel 13's Stat-Net conversion assumes 60% (its director says 72% would add two seats). Afkar's Jubran says 59-61%. The Joint List's internal poll shows 61%, and the parties target 70%. Surveys from before the lists formed gave 47-53% (Dayan Center, May 2026; Stat-Net, February 2025) and 59% for young Arabs (Afkar, January 2026). In Channel 13's Arab phone sample, 73-80% say they are certain to vote. The surveys' record is unbiased but noisy (Dayan Center 2015 +1.2 points, 2021 +15, 2022 -11 and -4; sd about 11), so a 60% signal moves the 58% prior by under half a point. New headwinds offset it. Arab localities have 89 fewer polling stations although their electorate grew 10%, so a station serves 672 voters there against 578 in Jewish localities. In peer-reviewed analogues, consolidation cut in-person turnout by 3 points and extra distance cut ballots by 2-5%, three times more in minority areas. Likud and Religious Zionism will post 2,000 activists at Arab stations; in 2019 a similar operation coincided with a record low and then a 10-point rebound. Balad's leader withdrew. Net: keep 58% and sd 0.05. At full pass-through one point of Arab turnout is worth about 0.2 seats; through k = 0.247, about 0.05.

Haredi sector. Here the 2026 evidence departs most from the model's assumptions. Channel 12's analyst reports internal polls showing about a 10% fall in haredi willingness to vote. UTJ's campaign is paralysed by a rabbinic rift; its chairman warned of a turnout drop. A Super Data poll has only 75% certain to vote (69% under 30). Self-reports depend on mode (Channel 13: 80% certain by phone, 66-67% online), and haredim always report less certainty than they show, so none of this is a measurement. IDI documents disputes costing UTJ in 2009, 2015 and 2021. The wartime 2024 local elections, by contrast, left haredi turnout flat. A 10% relative drop across about 630,000 haredi eligible voters is worth about one seat, the size of the model's haredi under-poll mean (0.98). The challenge proposes a downside tail or a shrunken mean, plus a kalpi test of whether haredi turnout dips predict the family error.

Jewish sector. 2022's rise was differential: right-leaning cities gained 3-7 points while centre-left cities stayed flat. Yet the right bloc's vote share moved only 1.3 points. Likud and Religious Zionism run a joint turnout operation; the tracking ban limits party machines. The correlated bloc swing covers this; no separate Jewish turnout term is warranted.

Envelopes and security. Double envelopes grew from 5.5% of ballots (2015) to 9.6% (2021). 2026 has at least 850 military stations (a quarter mobile, voting from 20 October), and special accessible (3,620) and hospital (250) stations are up on 2022, so the late-count rightward drift stays. The home-front emergency declaration runs to 3 November ('high probability' of attack, no restrictions in force); about 14,000 people remain displaced; no weather forecast exists yet.

findings.claim: The 2026 register is 8% larger than 2022's, with 12,018 polling stations. Election day is a paid national day of rest with free intercity buses and trains, the same arrangement as 2022, so the date itself adds no new turnout effect.
findings.quant: Eligible voters 7,331,981 (2022: 6,788,804), so +543,177 (+8.0%), the figure the article gives as voters 'added to the register since 2022' (it equals the net change). Polling stations 12,018; accessible 6,208, of which 3,620 special accessible stations (double-envelope capable); 250 hospital stations (hospitals with 50+ beds); 55 prison and detention stations; 102 stations in 100 missions abroad (state employees only). Hours 07:00-22:00 (small communities, hospitals, prisons, nursing homes 08:00-20:00). Day of rest under Basic Law: The Knesset; employees who work are paid 200%. Intercity buses (15 km+) and Israel Railways free from 26 Oct 20:00. Final results by 4 Nov. The CEC chairman's figure is reported elsewhere as 7,336,553 (secondary GitHub citation, not opened); Arutz 7 (14 Oct) gives '7.33 million' and 12,018 stations.

findings.site_use: 7,331,981 Israelis are eligible to vote on 27 October at 12,018 polling stations; election day is a paid day of rest with free intercity transport, as in 2022.

findings.claim: Against the 2022 baseline, 2026 has more stations of every special type, and double-envelope voting had already grown from 5.5% to 9.6% of ballots between 2015 and 2021. The official CEC-based Arab series differs from the Dayan Center series by up to about 2 points.
findings.quant: 2022 (Knesset fact sheet, 24 Oct 2022): eligible 6,788,804 (+210,720, +3.2% on 2021); 11,707 regular polling stations, 5,116 accessible, 2,939 special accessible; 222 hospital, 55 prison, 232 retirement-home, 414 COVID stations; 103 stations in 101 missions. Double-envelope ballots: 2015 234,599 (5.5%), Apr 2019 240,783 (5.5%), Sep 2019 282,442 (6.3%), 2020 330,209 (7.2%), 2021 425,512 (9.6%, COVID arrangements). National turnout 71.5 / 69.8 / 68.5 / 67.4 (2020 / Sep 2019 / Apr 2019 / 2021). Turnout by locality type, 21st-24th Knesset: Jews and others 71.9, 72.1, 73.2, 71.9; Arabs 50.0, 57.7, 62.9, 44.2 (read from the chart; the Dayan series gives 49.2, 59.2, 64.8, 44.6). 2026 vs 2022: special accessible stations +23% (3,620 vs 2,939), hospital stations +13% (250 vs 222). No official 2022 double-envelope total was located.

findings.site_use: Double-envelope ballots (soldiers, hospital patients, prisoners, voters at accessible stations) rose from 5.5% of ballots in 2015 to 9.6% in 2021 and are counted after election night.

findings.claim: Double-envelope ballots lean right and away from the Arab and haredi lists, so more envelope voting moves the final count rightward after election night. Soldiers are the largest group.
findings.quant: March 2021 envelopes: 425,512 (9.59% of all ballots). Netanyahu camp (with Yamina) 48.76% vs anti-Netanyahu camp 48.56% of envelope ballots. Religious Zionism more than 25% above its regular-station rate; Arab lists less than half their regular-station rate; Shas and UTJ about one third lower. Earlier counts: Apr 2019 240,783 (5.55%), Sep 2019 282,442 (6.32%), 2020 330,209 (7.15%). The authors note the soldier share has been falling as accessible stations are used more.

findings.claim: The IDF is running its largest field vote: at least 850 military polling stations, a quarter of them mobile, including positions in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria, with voting from the evening of 20 October. Inference: the soldier envelope pool is likely at least as large as in 2022.
findings.quant: At least 850 military stations; about one quarter fully mobile; military voting opens the evening of 20 Oct and stations stay open through 27 Oct; soldiers may also vote at civilian stations; about 3,000 soldiers (mostly conscripts) staff the stations, trained by the CEC. Haaretz (12 Oct, paywalled, not opened) reports about 100 more military stations than last time; the 2022 IDF turnout of 73% quoted in Israeli TV coverage could not be opened (unverified).

findings.site_use: Soldiers vote from 20 October at at least 850 military stations, a quarter of them mobile; their double-envelope ballots are counted after election night.

findings.claim: Special-population voting is small in seat terms. About 14,000 people are still displaced; nursing-home stations reached about 30,000 voters last time. Dedicated stations will serve the evacuated Gaza-border communities.
findings.quant: CEC at the Knesset committee (23 Jun 2026): about 14,000 people still displaced from their homes (about 0.2% of the register); a dedicated 'election address' was proposed. Nursing homes and sheltered housing last election: stations in 226 institutions, about 37,000 eligible, about 30,000 voted (about 81%). The CEC deputy director opposed permanent cameras in polling stations because they 'could discourage voters'. Per ynet's guide (15 Oct), dedicated stations will serve the communities evacuated from Be'eri, Kfar Aza, Nir Oz and Holit; evacuees may also vote at their original station or an accessible station.

source.access: opened

findings.model_link: None directly; bounds the evacuee effect on turnout as negligible (<0.1 seat).

findings.claim: Net emigration since 2022 inflates the register's denominator. About 125,000 more Israelis left long-term than returned between January 2022 and August 2024, and those still registered lower measured turnout by about 1.2 points if nothing else changes.
findings.quant: CBS data compiled by the Knesset Research and Information Center: long-term departures 59,400 (2022) and 82,800 (2023, +39%); returns 29,600 (2022) and 24,200 (2023). Net migration balance of Israelis -29,700 (2022), -58,600 (2023), -36,900 (Jan-Aug 2024); cumulative about -125,200 since the start of 2022. Inference (this desk): if these adults stay on the roll and do not vote, 2022-level behaviour gives 70.6 x 125,200 / 7,331,981, about a 1.2-point lower measured turnout. The roll may also lose people marked 'ceased to be resident' (code 51); no official total was found.

findings.claim: Arab localities have 89 fewer polling stations than in 2022, although their electorate grew about 10%. In 2026 an average Arab-locality station serves 672 voters against 578 in Jewish localities; in 2021 the two were about equal.
findings.quant: Stat-Net position paper and appendix, from CEC station lists as of 31 May 2026: Arab-locality stations 1,628 (2022) to 1,539 (2026), -89; Jewish-locality stations 7,886 to 8,482, +596. Eligible voters in Arab localities about +96,000 (+10.2%) vs +8.1% in Jewish localities. Voters per station 672 vs 578 (gap about 16%); 2021: about 528 vs 539. 52 of 147 Arab localities (35%) have fewer stations despite more voters (Jewish localities: 3%). Examples: Kafr Bana 15 to 9 stations (6,492 eligible); Ma'ar 31 to 25. Stat-Net: about 250 more Arab-locality stations would close the gap. Unrecognised Negev villages: 30-45 minutes' travel; some tribal assignments up to 65 km. The CEC says the Interior Ministry places stations through the CBS. Inference: 938,401 (2022 Arab and Druze eligible, Bayan 28) x 1.102 gives about 1.03 million Arab-locality eligible voters in 2026, about 14.1% of the register.

source.title: Elections 2026: more Arab voters at fewer polling stations (Hebrew)
source.access: opened; the Stat-Net paper itself was not located

findings.model_link: ARAB_TURNOUT['mean_unified'] (0.58): a new 2026 headwind outside the regime table; KALPI_ARAB_CAP denominator (Arab eligible about 1.03m).

findings.claim: Peer-reviewed natural-experiment evidence: consolidating polling places cut overall turnout by 1.85 points, and in-person turnout by 3.03 points. Israel has no civilian absentee voting to absorb the loss, so the in-person figure is the closer analogue.
findings.quant: Los Angeles County, 2003 California gubernatorial recall (precinct consolidation): overall turnout -1.85 points, polling-place turnout -3.03, absentee +1.18. Both transport costs and search costs (finding the new place) contributed; Democrats responded more. Transfer to Israel is an analogy, not a measurement: Arab-locality station load rose about 16% relative to Jewish localities (TRN-F07).

source.authors: Henry E. Brady; John E. McNulty

findings.model_link: ARAB_TURNOUT mean: size of a possible station-load adjustment.

findings.claim: Peer-reviewed boundary-discontinuity evidence: one standard deviation more distance to the polling place (0.245 miles) cuts ballots cast by 2-5%. The effect is about three times larger in high-minority areas in lower-salience elections.
findings.quant: Nine municipalities in Massachusetts and Minnesota, four elections (2012-2016): +1 sd distance gives -2% to -5% of ballots; in non-presidential elections the effect is about 3x in high-minority vs low-minority areas. The paper's counterfactuals remove the distance effect for +1.6 to +4 points turnout. A Knesset election is high-salience (closer to the presidential case, where the minority gap was not significant), so the upper end is unlikely to apply.

findings.claim: Likud and Religious Zionism say they will station about 2,000 activists at hundreds of polling stations in Arab communities, on top of the formal observers, citing fraud claims the CEC has rejected. The 2019 precedent cuts both ways. A similar camera operation in April 2019 coincided with a record-low Arab turnout, which its organiser claimed as his doing, though no independent study links the two. Five months later Arab turnout rebounded 10 points.
findings.quant: 2026 (announced 15 Oct, D-12): nearly 2,000 activists (Haaretz: religious-nationalist activists and yeshiva students); 'hundreds of polling stations' chosen by a 'special mapping' of fraud risk; no official function. CEC director Dean Livne in June: 'There is no fraud in Israel. If it exists, it is on the margins.' 2019 (Times of Israel, Jacob Magid, 8 Aug 2019): about 1,200 activists with hidden body cameras, about 40 coordinators; the organiser posted that 'voter turnout dropped below 50%'. IDI: Arab turnout 49.2% (Apr 2019) vs 63.8% (2015, IDI basis). Police investigated only two stations, neither targeted by Likud. Likud doubled the budget to about NIS 2 million for September 2019, when Arab turnout was 59.2% (Dayan series, SEC-F01). Neither article gives a causal estimate.

source.title: Likud, Smotrich to station 2,000 activists at Arab polling stations on election day, citing unsubstantiated concerns of fraud

findings.model_link: ARAB_TURNOUT spread (0.05): an event that can move Arab turnout either way. No directional intimidation term; the precedent supports a symmetric spread.

findings.claim: Channel 13's Arab seat numbers assume 60% Arab turnout, according to the head of Stat-Net, which fields its Arab sample. He says 72% would lift the Arab lists from 14 to 16 seats, about 0.17 seats per point at full pass-through. This answers the sector desk's open question on Channel 13's conversion.
findings.quant: Channel 13 poll published 3 Sep 2026: Joint List 9, Ra'am 5 at a 60% Arab-turnout assumption (Yousef Makladeh, Stat-Net). At 72% with all else equal: Joint List 10, Ra'am 6. If Amcha Yisrael fails the threshold: Joint List 11, Ra'am 6-7. Desk arithmetic for comparison: 1 point of Arab-locality turnout is about 10,300 voters x 0.858 Arab-list share (2022), about 8,900 votes, about 0.22 seats at about 40,000 votes per seat. Through the model's k = 0.247 that is about 0.05 seats per point. Makladeh (Kul al-Arab interview, 28 Apr 2026) also said a four-party list would 'automatically' add about 10 points of turnout.

findings.quant: Dr. Hisham Jubran (Afkar), for i24NEWS Arabic (article undated, after the CEC disqualification votes; Oct 2026): expected Arab turnout 59-61%. He reads the exclusion attempts as a mobiliser. Arab support for Zionist 'change' parties, especially the Democrats, reportedly fell because they backed the disqualifications. 'About 15 seats would require at least 65%.' No sample size or dates given. Afkar's September filing converts at 60% (SEC-F09).

findings.claim: The parties' own numbers are higher still: the Joint List's internal poll shows 61% two weeks out, and the list and Hadash both target 70%. Activist reports also cut both ways: more willingness to vote overall, but Balad's base was demobilised when its leader withdrew under threat of disqualification.
findings.quant: Local Call, 12 Oct 2026: Joint List internal poll about two weeks before election day projects 61% Arab turnout; target near 70%; no pollster, n or dates. Field activists (Yafia; Standing Together in the Southern Triangle) report more willingness to vote. Sami Abu Shehadeh's withdrawal 'reduced motivation among some Balad activists'; others say the threat raises motivation. Al-Araby (4 Oct): Hadash secretary-general Amjad Shbeita is 'working toward 70%', which he says would give the Joint List more than 10 seats.

findings.claim: Channel 13's sector samples (official CEC filings) give stated certainty of voting by sector over the last three waves. The Arab phone sample's 'certain' share is 73-80%, flat within noise. The haredi share depends on mode: 80% by phone, 66-67% online. Haredim report the least certainty, as in past cycles, so stated certainty cannot rank sectors by turnout.
findings.quant: Question: 'Will you vote or not on election day?' (raw, unweighted). 22-23 Sep (filing 4169): Arab n=100 phone, certain 80.2 / fairly sure 6.4 / not so sure 7.4 / good chance not 6.0; haredi phone n=220, 80.0 / 9.5; haredi online n=293, 67.2 / 20.8; adult Jews n=1,001, 73.0 / 15.7. 29-30 Sep (4182): Arab n=122, 73.0 / 16.4 / 0.8 / 9.8; haredi online n=230, 67.0 / 21.7; adult Jews n=600, 73.0 / 18.5. 6-7 Oct (4193): Arab n=100 (439 called, 22.8% complete), 78.0 / 15.0 / 2.0 / 5.0; haredi online n=500, 66.2 / 21.2 / 4.8 / 6.4; adult Jews n=603, 74.6 / 16.3. 6-7 Oct vote question, Arab sample: Joint List 42%, Ra'am 33%, undecided 10%, won't vote 5%; haredi sample: UTJ 49.2%, Shas 17.6%, The Haredi Public 5.2%, Tzeva Shachor 0.6%, won't vote 5.0%, undecided 8.6%. Seats are converted 'by sector weights in the population' (Prof. David Steinberg).

findings.claim: Afkar's survey of young Arabs for the Abraham Initiatives (January 2026, before the lists formed) projects 59% turnout among 18-34s. Stated intention collapses among past abstainers and first-time voters, the groups whose turnout decides the sector.
findings.quant: Fieldwork 20-27 Jan 2026; 614 young adults aged 18-34; quota sample by age, gender, region and religion; the slide gives 388 phone and 266 digital responses, which sum to 654, not 614 (internal inconsistency). 'If Knesset elections were held today, would you vote?' Past voters: 70% definitely; past abstainers: 15% definitely, 42% probably; first-time voters: 43% definitely. Estimated turnout 59% from a 'Motivation Model' combining intentions, importance of voting and past behaviour. 54% say voting is important or very important (50% of first-time voters); 27% say few or none of their close friends vote.

findings.claim: Stat-Net's February 2025 Arab survey for the Abraham Initiatives ran two turnout models on the same data: 53% and 47%. A 6-point spread from modelling choice alone, before the list configuration was known.
findings.quant: n=750, telephone in Arabic, 10-17 Feb 2025, sample weighted by previous voting patterns, religion and geography. Expected turnout 53% ('Bias Model'); 47% under the 'Motivation Model', which drives all of its demographic breakdowns. Abraham Initiatives summary: 89% support a four-party joint list; 18% name division among Arab parties as the top barrier to voting; 30% name lack of impact.

findings.claim: The Dayan Center's unity-year forecast for 2015 was close (64.7% expected vs 63.5% actual). With the misses the sector desk recorded, the four KAP forecasts that could be checked have a mean error near zero and a spread of about 11 points: unbiased but very noisy.
findings.quant: KAP / Moshe Dayan Center, February 2015, n=500: expected turnout 64.7%, then the highest since 1999; 44.8% said the Hadash-Balad-Ra'am-Ta'al union 'significantly influenced' their decision to vote; Joint List 13 seats. Actual: 63.5% (Dayan series), 13 seats; error +1.2. With SEC-F07 (Mar 2021 +15.1, Aug 2022 -11.2, Oct 2022 -4.2): four KAP errors, mean +0.2, sd about 11.1 points. Separately, a 2015 Yafa Institute poll for the Abraham Fund put ideological boycotters at no more than 17% of Arab non-voters (about 3% of the Arab public).

'Do you intend to vote in the upcoming Knesset elections?': Arabs 62% certain + 25% think so = 87%; Jews 63% + 29% = 92%; total 63% + 28%. Secular Jews are most emphatic (72% certain); the chart reads about 52% certain for haredim. The English summary gives n=576 (443 Jews, 133 Arabs), which differs from the Hebrew PDF.

findings.claim: A geo-demographic analysis counts a record 595,000 first-time voters (8.7% of the register): about 118,000 Arab (10.6% of the Arab sector) and about 105,000 haredi (one in six haredi eligible voters). The haredi figure implies about 630,000 haredi eligible voters. The source's total register (6.8m) conflicts with the CEC's 7.33m, so treat its counts as approximate.
findings.quant: Points Location Intelligence, via the Jerusalem Post (23 Jul 2026): 595,000 aged 18-22 first-time voters, about 8.7% of eligible voters; haredi sector about 105,000 new voters, 'one in every six eligible voters in the haredi sector'; Arab sector more than 118,000, 10.6% of Arab-sector eligible. Implied (desk arithmetic): haredi eligible about 630,000; Arab-sector eligible about 1.11m (wider than the 1.03m Arab-locality count in TRN-F07, since it includes mixed cities). The same piece gives 6.8m total eligible (+9.4% on 'about 6.2m' in 2022); the CEC numbers are 7,331,981 and 6,788,804.

findings.claim: IDI's August 2026 Voice Index: only 1.2% of Jews and 8.7% of Arabs volunteer that they do not intend to vote, against actual non-voting of roughly 28% and 47% in 2022. Crime in Arab society is the top vote factor for Arab respondents.
findings.quant: Fieldwork 31 Aug-3 Sep 2026 (Shiluv I2R), 605 Jews and 150 Arabs, max error +/-3.57%. Q7 'What will have the greatest influence on your decision regarding which party to vote for?': 'Don't intend to vote' 2.4% total / 1.2% Jews / 8.7% Arabs. Arabs: crime in Arab society 31.5% first factor (53.5% first or second), economy 18.9% (46% first or second). October 7 'very' or 'fairly central' to the vote: 68.3% of Jews, 32.3% of Arabs. Security outlook 'very pessimistic': Arabs 46.4%, Jews 21.2%.

findings.claim: Channel 12's analyst reports haredi parties' internal polls showing about a 10% fall in willingness to vote. UTJ's campaign headquarters is paralysed by a rift between the two leading Lithuanian rabbis, and Shas is losing voters over the draft-exemption stance, some of whom are staying home.
findings.quant: N12, 11-12 Oct 2026: Shas+UTJ won 18 seats in 2022 and poll 14-15; demographic growth 'could have been expected' to give 19-20. 'Internal polls show about a 10% drop in the willingness of haredi voters to go to the polls.' UTJ: no campaign or mobilisation activity; senior officials say 8 seats would be a 'miracle' and 6 would not surprise them. Shas: some voters with family in the IDF are moving to Yesh Atid or Otzma or staying home. Corroboration: UTJ chairman Yaakov Asher, in closed-door remarks recorded by Kan (Arutz 7, 6 Oct), warned that haredi turnout could fall and that 'four years ... means tens of thousands of votes' that must reach the ballot box.

findings.quant: Super Data (chairman Avi Weidman), published 14 Oct 2026: 75% 'certainly will vote'; 69% under 30. Reasons for not voting: 36% 'existing haredi parties don't represent me', 33% won't vote for another party against the rabbis' view. Under-30 support: Shas 13% (previously 33-36%); UTJ 41% (previously 50%; age group unclear); Leitner (The Haredi Public) 11%; Achi 9% (12% of young). 62% believe activists control the homes of the leading rabbis. Sample size, dates and wording not stated.

findings.claim: IDI's haredi specialists document that internal disputes have cost UTJ before, in 2009, 2015 and 2021, and that haredi party loyalty is far higher than the public's. Haredi turnout dips are tied to rabbinic disputes, not just demography.
findings.quant: 2009: internal disputes cost UTJ a seat (its only such loss). 2015: part of the Jerusalem Faction abstained on rabbinic instruction and UTJ's share fell in strongly haredi areas. 2021: UTJ's share fell amid resentment over COVID conduct. 2025 Democracy Index: 36% of haredim will vote for the same party as before vs 7% of the general public; 41% cite religion-and-state as the main factor (vs 17%). June 2026 Voice Index: 28% rate the haredi leadership highly on advancing voters' interests. Demographic growth since 2013 'has the potential to finally bring an eighth seat'.

findings.claim: The Jerusalem Faction (Peleg), which has abstained since 2015, tried in August to split Gur from UTJ into a hard anti-draft list to draw non-voting haredim; Gur refused. A separate anti-draft list (Tzeva Shachor) is on the ballot but polls near zero. No haredi vehicle is drawing new voters in, so draft anger shows up as abstention, not as a new list.
findings.quant: N12, 16 Aug 2026: the Faction and allied rabbis proposed that Gur leave UTJ for a separate party with a hardline anti-conscription stance, aiming for 'an extra seat' from people who do not vote now; Gur's Moti Bebchik rejected it. Srugim, 15 Aug: 'Tzeva Shachor' (named for a draft-alert line with about 100,000 subscribers), organisers claim potential support in the 'tens of thousands'. Channel 13 haredi sample, 6-7 Oct (TRN-F14): Tzeva Shachor 0.6%, The Haredi Public 5.2%. A June 2026 report of 'about 40,000 Peleg voters will not vote' surfaced in search results but was not opened (unverified).

Likud and Religious Zionism have set up a joint election-day operation to raise right-wing turnout, headed by the Yesha Council chairman, while the High Court's ban on real-time voter tracking (SEC-F21) limits the party machines' traditional tool.
findings.quant: Times of Israel, 7 Oct 2026: Netanyahu and Smotrich hold a joint 'Saving the Right' conference with Religious Zionist rabbis and yeshiva heads; the parties are setting up a joint operation to raise right-wing turnout, headed by Yesha Council chairman Israel Gantz (Channel 12). Otzma Yehudit was not invited; Likud signed a surplus agreement with RZP the day before. No scale or budget published.

findings.claim: In 2022 turnout rose 3.2 points overall, and the rise was differential: right-leaning cities gained 3-7 points while centre-left cities stayed flat. The right-wing bloc's vote share rose only 1.3 points; its 64 seats came mostly from wasted centre-left votes.
findings.quant: National turnout 67.4% (2021) to 70.6% (2022); Arab 44.6% to 53.2% (2020: 64.8%). Change vs 2021: Ashkelon +3.2, Beer Sheva +4.6, Dimona +6.9; Tel Aviv +0.4, Givatayim +0.3, Herzliya +0.3. Bloc vote shares: right 48.3% to 49.6%; centre-left 41.5% to 38.3%; Arab 8.6% to 10.8%; coalition 64 seats. Balad and Yamina-Jewish Home fell below the threshold.

findings.claim: Peer-reviewed locality analysis of 2022 (all 1,215 localities): settlements in Judea and Samaria and localities with many haredim have higher turnout; development towns and larger localities lower. Distance from the centre matters only in Arab localities.
findings.quant: Eight socio-demographic and geographic predictors, 2019-2022: SES predicts turnout in both Jewish/mixed and Arab localities; peripherality is not significant in Jewish and mixed localities but is significant in Arab localities; locality size is inversely related to turnout; development towns lower; Judea and Samaria and high-haredi-share localities higher. National turnout about 70%.

findings.claim: The only wartime election held since October 2023, the February 2024 municipal elections, saw turnout fall most among Arabs (-10 points vs 2018) and non-haredi Jews (-4.5), and hardly at all among haredim (-0.5). Election day was a holiday both times.
findings.quant: IDI analysis of the 2024 local elections: turnout in 2024 was lower than in 2018 but higher than in 2003, 2008 and 2013; change from 2018: Arab localities -10 points, non-haredi Jewish localities -4.5, haredi localities -0.5. Arab local turnout stayed close to the haredi level. Proposed reasons: the war diverted attention (haredim less affected, as few serve). Closing-night national turnout was about 49% vs 59.5% in 2018 (press figure, not in the IDI text).

findings.claim: The security backdrop is live but not restrictive. The government is extending the nationwide 'special situation on the home front' to 3 November, past election day, citing a 'high probability' of attack from Iran or Lebanon. No binding civil-defence restrictions are in force, and the CEC has emergency procedures for sirens during voting and counting.
findings.quant: Current declaration (in force since February) was due to expire 20 Oct; the Defence Minister asked to extend it to 3 Nov, with Knesset FADC approval needed. Defence officials: 'still a high probability' of an attack on the civilian population; uncertainty mainly on the Iranian and Lebanese fronts. The declaration lets Home Front Command restrict schools and gatherings, but 'no such directives are currently in effect'. CEC logistics (Arutz 7, 14 Oct): emergency kits let poll workers move counting to a protected space; asked whether a confrontation with Iran could cancel the vote, the logistics chief said it is 'not a logistical issue'.

findings.claim: Crime is the Arab public's top issue and the 2026 campaign's main Arab mobiliser. A general strike over police failures preceded the four Arab parties' January unity pledge, and killings remain at record levels.
findings.quant: Times of Israel, 22 Jan 2026: nationwide Arab general strike and Sakhnin march over police failure to curb violent crime; 2025 was the deadliest year on record (252 homicide victims). The same day the four parties signed a pact in Sakhnin (JNS and Jewish Chronicle reports, not opened); Ra'am later ran separately. AP (15 Oct 2026, opened): the Abraham Initiatives count 184 crime-related killings in Arab communities so far in 2026; 12% of first-half killings solved. IDI Aug 2026: crime the top vote factor (TRN-F20).

challenges.title: Arab turnout centre: keep 58%, but register the 2026 station-load headwind as a testable adjustment
challenges.what_literature_says: Post-formation 2026 estimates cluster at 59-61% (TRN-F11, F12; parties 61-70%, F13). Sector turnout surveys are unbiased but noisy (four KAP forecasts: mean error +0.2, sd about 11; F17, SEC-F07), so a 60% signal against a 58% prior with sd 5 moves the centre by about +0.3 point. Against that: 89 fewer Arab-locality stations and 16% more voters per station (F07); peer-reviewed consolidation and distance effects of 1.85-3 points and 2-5% of ballots, larger in minority areas (F08, F09); 2,000 partisan activists at Arab stations (F10; 2019 precedent ambiguous, F10); Balad's leader withdrew (F13); wartime local elections cut Arab turnout by 10 points (F28).
challenges.current_model: ARAB_TURNOUT['mean_unified'] = 0.580 (table-B mean), sd 0.05 (t, df 5), pass-through k = 0.247, intercept -0.634; base 0.538 (kalpi).
challenges.proposed_change: No change to the mean or sd now. The survey signal (+0.3) and the station-load headwind (plausibly -0.5 to -1.5 points) roughly cancel, and through k the stakes are about 0.05 seats per point. Pre-register one optional arm: a station-load adjustment, if and only if the kalpi panel shows within-locality turnout falls when voters per station rise. Update the site sentence to cite the 59-61% cluster and the station cut.
challenges.how_to_test: Kalpi panel 2019a-2022 (CEC station-level files): in Arab localities, regress the change in locality turnout on the change in voters per station (locality fixed effects, cycle dummies). Apply the coefficient to 2026's +16% relative load only if significant. Separately, grade an arm with T centre = KAP's final pre-election 'expected turnout' (available for 2015, 2021, 2022) against the table-B mean on the eight-cycle harness.

challenges.title: Haredi family mean in a turnout-stress year: add a downside tail or shrink the under-poll
challenges.what_literature_says: Internal party polls show about a 10% fall in haredi willingness to vote; UTJ's campaign is paralysed; the chairman warned of a turnout drop (F21). Super Data: 75% certain (69% under 30) (F22). IDI: rabbinic disputes cost UTJ votes in 2009, 2015 and 2021 (F23). The Jerusalem Faction offers no new vehicle (F24). Counter-evidence: haredim always under-report certainty (F14: 66-67% online vs 80% by phone; F18: lowest certainty among first-time voters), and wartime 2024 local elections left haredi turnout flat (F28). Arithmetic: a 10% relative drop across about 630,000 haredi eligible voters (F19) is about 48,000 voters, about 41,000 haredi-list votes, about 1 seat.
challenges.current_model: FAMILY_SHOCK['haredi'] = (-0.98 e0, sd 1.77) seats: the projection adds about one seat to Shas+UTJ over the polls; s.4 haredi turnout 78-82% 'near-invariant with a small protest-under-vote tail'.
challenges.proposed_change: Do not let the historical under-count carry into 2026 unexamined. Option A: a mixture tail. With p of about 0.25, a haredi turnout dip worth -1 seat replaces the -0.98 mean in that branch, so the expected under-count is about -0.5. Option B: shrink the mean to about -0.5 and keep sd 1.77. Allocate the tail mostly to UTJ: Shas's loss is to other lists, which polls already see. Either is disclosed judgement unless the test below supports it.
challenges.how_to_test: Build the haredi-cluster turnout series from kalpi and CEC locality results (Bnei Brak, Elad, Beitar Illit, Modiin Illit, haredi Jerusalem stations) for all eight cycles. Regress the haredi family e0 on the turnout deviation from trend. A positive slope (low turnout, smaller under-poll) significant at 2 se would justify a turnout-linked term; 2021 (turnout dip 72.8, e1 -1.33) is the key cycle and argues against. Report the 2026 effect either way.

challenges.title: No separate Jewish-sector turnout term
challenges.what_literature_says: 2022's turnout rise was concentrated in right-leaning localities (+3 to +7 vs about 0 in the centre-left), but the right bloc's vote share rose only 1.3 points (F26). Settlements and haredi localities vote more (F27). Both camps run turnout operations in 2026 (F25), and the tracking ban limits machines (SEC-F21).
challenges.current_model: Correlated bloc swing (t, df 5) x event risk 1.2; gevalt coupling.
challenges.proposed_change: None. Differential Jewish turnout is a bloc-level phenomenon of about one point of share, which the bloc swing's spread already covers.
challenges.how_to_test: From the kalpi panel, compute each cycle's realised differential turnout (right-leaning minus centre-left Jewish localities, vs the previous cycle) and correlate it with the harness bloc-swing residual over 2019a-2022 (and 2009-2015 from CEC locality files). Add a term only if |r| > 0.6 across at least six cycles.

challenges.title: National turnout prior: account for the emigration denominator
challenges.what_literature_says: Net emigration of about 125,000 Israelis (2022 to Aug 2024) stays on the register, which mechanically lowers measured turnout by about 1.2 points at 2022 behaviour (F06). The register grew 8.0% (F01). Wartime local elections lost 4.5-10 points outside the haredi sector (F28); a Knesset election is far more salient.
challenges.proposed_change: Centre at about 69.5-70.0 with the same spread, or state on the site that the register includes emigrants. Seats are allocated on shares, so the stake is only threshold arithmetic in votes.
challenges.how_to_test: No harness test needed. After the election, compare realised turnout with the prior and the denominator estimate.

challenges.title: Self-reported certainty is not a sector turnout signal
challenges.what_literature_says: Stated non-voting is tiny (Jews 1.2%, Arabs 8.7%) against actual abstention of about 28% and 47% (F20). Haredi certainty depends on mode (80 phone vs 67 online) and ranks sectors backwards (F14, F18).
challenges.current_model: Certainty layer (soft support churn, undecided lean) uses per-list certainty; s.20 decided not to drive turnout from surveys.
challenges.proposed_change: Keep sector turnout out of the certainty layer. If the haredi certainty columns from Channel 13 are ever ingested, use the phone sample or mode-adjust.
challenges.how_to_test: Evidence class: survey methodology; no record exists for Channel 13's certainty question before 2026. Re-check after the election.

open_questions: No weather forecast for 27 Oct exists at D-11, and no Israeli study of weather effects on Knesset turnout was found. Check the Israel Meteorological Service around 24 Oct.

No KAP, IDI or Stat-Net Arab turnout survey fielded after the Supreme Court ruling (2 Oct) was found. KAP published final surveys about a week out in 2021 and 2022; watch for one around 20 Oct and read it against its error record (sd about 11 points).
Will the CEC regulate the 2,000 Likud-RZP activists (no official role) at Arab stations? A ruling or police guidance before 27 Oct would bear on the intimidation risk.

Official 2022 double-envelope total and the 2022 IDF turnout (73% is quoted on Israeli TV; the i24 page could not be opened) were not located. Haaretz's 'about 100 more military stations than last time' is paywalled and unverified.

The CEC chairman's eligible-voter figure is cited as 7,336,553 (secondary GitHub citation, not opened) against ynet's 7,331,981. The difference (4,572) may be a snapshot date or the diplomatic register; confirm from the CEC notice.
No 2026-specific turnout evidence was found for Druze or Russian-speaking voters (a Haaretz feature on Golan Druze preparing to vote was paywalled).
The number of dedicated evacuee polling stations for 2026 was not found; only the communities served (Be'eri, Kfar Aza, Nir Oz, Holit) are named.
Haredi internal polls (N12, 11 Oct) and the Super Data poll publish no sample size, dates or wording; the haredi turnout signal rests on unpublished data.
Afkar's youth survey prints n=614 but 388 phone + 266 digital = 654; ask the Abraham Initiatives which is right.
